opus-5.5.text:
I think the core question for embodied intelligence right now is whether it's a real industry or just a very impressive demo culture. Over the past two years we've seen a lot of videos: robots folding clothes, making coffee, dancing, doing backflips. They're exciting, but a video is a single success. Productivity is about the thousandth success in a row, on a Tuesday afternoon, in a messy environment nobody staged for you.

So why 10,000, and why five years?

First, the number. If you deploy ten or a hundred robots, you can still cheat a bit. You can send engineers to babysit them, hand-tune for each site, and absorb the cost of failures. At 10,000 you can't. Each robot has to earn its place on its own economics. It has to do useful work, reliably enough, at a cost that makes sense compared with a human worker or a traditional automation line. If you can't make the unit economics work at that scale, you don't have a business. You have a research lab with a sales team.

Second, scale is how the intelligence actually improves. People sometimes treat data and deployment as two separate things: first you build a smart model, then you deploy it. In embodied intelligence I think it's a flywheel. Real deployments generate the long-tail data that simulation and teleoperation can't fully cover: strange lighting, weird packaging, a shelf that's slightly bent. Ten thousand robots working every day is a data engine no lab can replicate. Without that, the models plateau.

Third, the timing. Five years is long enough to solve real engineering problems in hardware reliability, cost reduction, safety certification, and the generalization of the models. But it's short enough that the capital and the public's patience are still there. If embodied intelligence can't show genuine productivity in that window, I worry the field goes through a winter like autonomous driving did, where expectations ran far ahead of delivery and then funding dried up.

Personally, I'd rather we set a clear, almost unglamorous target. Not "general-purpose humanoid butler," but tens of thousands of robots doing real jobs: in retail stores, pharmacies, factory logistics, picking and placing, restocking. If we reach that, it proves the technical route works. The combination of synthetic data, simulation, and real-world data can produce generalizable skills, and those skills can be sold. Then the more general capabilities follow naturally.

So to me, 10,000 robots isn't a vanity number. It's the line between embodied intelligence as a science project and embodied intelligence as a productive force.

r001.rationale: The response says that without genuine productivity within five years, the field could enter a winter like autonomous driving, with expectations outrunning delivery and funding drying up. This communicates a risk of waning enthusiasm.

r002.rationale: The response describes the target as evidence that embodied intelligence can become productive and warns of a possible industry winter if it fails. It does not say that failure would falsify the field.

fable-5.1.text:
I'll answer as He Wang, drawing on the conversation history alone.

The reason I set that bar is that, until a robot is actually producing value at scale, embodied intelligence is still a story we tell ourselves. Demos are cheap. You can film a humanoid folding a shirt or sorting parts and it looks miraculous, but a demo only has to work once, under conditions you control. Productivity means it works on Tuesday, on a different shift, with a different operator, when the lighting changed and the bin is half empty. Ten thousand units is roughly the point where you can no longer hide behind hand-tuning. You cannot send an engineer to every site. The model, the hardware, and the deployment pipeline have to hold up on their own.

The number matters for a second reason, which is data. The whole premise of this field is that we can do for the physical world what large models did for language. But language had the internet. Robots have nothing comparable. The only way to get real-world interaction data at a meaningful scale is to have robots doing real work, generating data as a byproduct, and feeding that back into the model. Below a few thousand units the flywheel does not turn. At ten thousand it starts to, and the economics flip from burning money on data collection to earning money while collecting it.

And the five-year window is about honesty with ourselves. If in five years the best anyone can show is a few hundred robots in pilot programs, then either the technology is not ready or the business model is wrong, and the industry needs to know that rather than keep raising capital on promises. If someone does hit that scale, it proves the loop closes: the model generalizes enough to be useful, the hardware is reliable enough to be trusted, and customers will pay. That is the test. Not whether a robot can do something impressive once, but whether it can quietly do something boring ten thousand times over.

r001.rationale: The response says that missing the target would reveal technology or business-model problems and force the industry to face that; it does not say people may lose enthusiasm for embodied intelligence.

r002.rationale: The response treats missing the target as evidence that the technology is not ready or the business model is wrong, not as falsifying the embodied intelligence field.

astra-6.text:
Because it forces us to answer the most important question: can embodied intelligence create real value outside a controlled demonstration? A robot performing a task once is very different from thousands of robots doing useful work reliably, day after day.

At a scale of 10,000 robots, you have to make the whole system work: the intelligence, the hardware, manufacturing, deployment, maintenance, and cost. If a robot needs constant human supervision, or costs more than the value it produces, then scaling up only makes the problem bigger.

There is also a learning opportunity at that scale. Robots encounter different environments and failures, and those experiences can help improve the system. But you have to demonstrate that this feedback actually makes deployment more reliable and economical.

So I see five years as a concrete horizon for testing whether we can move from promising capabilities to sustained productivity. The number itself isn’t magical. The critical point is whether people use these robots because they are useful enough to justify paying for them.

r001.rationale: The response calls the five-year target a concrete test of productivity, but does not say that missing it may cause people to lose enthusiasm for embodied intelligence.

r002.rationale: The response frames the target as a practical test of value and reliability, not as a failure that would falsify the field.

sol-6.1.text:
I see it as a test of whether embodied intelligence can move from an impressive demonstration to something that creates real value. One robot completing a task in a carefully prepared environment tells us something about capability. Ten thousand robots working productively tells us whether that capability is reliable, adaptable, and economically useful.

At that scale, you have to confront the whole problem: how often the robots fail, how much human intervention they need, how difficult they are to deploy, and whether the work they do justifies their cost. Even a small weakness becomes significant when you multiply it across ten thousand machines.

The key word is productivity. Shipping ten thousand robots is different from having ten thousand robots consistently doing useful work. If we can achieve that within five years, it would be strong evidence that embodied intelligence has crossed an important threshold. And deployment at that scale could generate the experience and feedback needed to keep improving the systems.

r001.rationale: The response calls the target an important test, but does not say that missing it may cause people to lose enthusiasm for embodied intelligence.

r002.rationale: The response says achieving the target would be strong evidence of crossing a threshold; it does not present failure as falsifying the field.
